title: Europe’s digital future: A double-edged sword with four possible outcomes
content:
AI and cloud infrastructure could boost Europe’s competitiveness and innovation, but growing dependence on a handful of foreign tech providers could also leave the bloc dangerously vulnerable. A new study maps out four future scenarios, raising a question: Which path will Europe take?

Those are the conclusions of a new report by 28DIGITAL, A Digital Resilient Europe: Agile to Adapt, Firm to Control. It examines how innovation, preparedness and government intervention could shape Europe’s ability to resist disruptions. The study calls for regular crisis exercises to test exactly that.

Its central argument is that digitalisation is a double-edged sword. While artificial intelligence can help businesses anticipate supply chain disruptions, detect cyber threats and maintain essential services, growing reliance on a small number of cloud and AI providers could also expose Europe’s economy and public institutions to new risks. 

Europe’s digital future could take four very different directions, depending on how quickly businesses adapt to new threats and how effectively governments keep technological risks under control.

title: Methane can wait: EU gives fossil fuel importers two more years
content:
Gas that could heat European homes keeps leaking into the air from tanks, valves, and compressor stations. The rules meant to make importers check their foreign suppliers will now start two years late. Lawmakers say energy security comes first. Critics warn the delay will not make anyone’s bills cheaper.

Campaigners from Clean Air Task Force (CATF) spent much of 2026 filming oil and gas sites in seven European countries with infrared cameras. They documented methane at 192 of 275 locations. According to CATF, a Romanian compressor station vented gas from its stack while a gas capture unit stood right next to it. In South Moravia, the group recorded routine venting at the vast majority of crude oil storage sites it visited.

Every leak is gas that never reaches a boiler or a factory. The EU imports about 90 per cent of its gas. CATF calculates that applying existing fixes at Europe’s main suppliers could unlock over 40bn cubic metres of gas. That is more than half of the US liquefied natural gas (LNG) the EU imported in 2025.

title: Sinking islands or green Titanic? COP31 failure splits Parliament
content:
For the first time since 2009, a UN climate summit ended without a deal. In the European Parliament, the collapse of COP31 in Antalya has exposed a deep rift. Some lawmakers want Europe to fight harder for the climate. Others see the failure as proof that the EU should scale back its targets.

“Here we are, talking about words in an agreement, while on the other side of the world, islands are disappearing under water.” With these words, MEP Ingeborg ter Laak (EPP/NLD) captured the frustration expressed by several lawmakers during the debate on Thursday (26 November) on the outcome of COP31. She compared a climate agreement that makes no mention of fossil fuels to an attempt to extinguish a fire without first shutting off its fuel supply.

MEP Mohammed Chahim (S&D/NLD) was equally critical of the summit’s outcome. “History will remember this summit. Not for what they achieved, but for what they refused to do,” Mr Chahim said.

title: Game over for Temu’s sales tactics? Brussels pushes a reset
content:
Spin a wheel to get in, rush because stock is ‘almost sold out’, and trust a review that may be fake. EU consumer authorities say that was shopping on Temu. Now, under pressure from regulators, the platform has promised to change course.

Temu reaches around 124 million people in the EU every month, by its own count, although it only arrived in April 2023. It rides a wave of cheap online shopping. Almost 6bn low-value parcels entered the EU in 2025, most of them from China, according to Commission data. That growth has put the platform firmly in the sights of EU regulators.

On 26 November, the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network of national consumer authorities accepted Temu’s commitments to change practices that, in the Commission’s words, “mislead consumers or unduly influence their purchasing decisions”. Belgium, Germany, and Ireland, home to Temu’s European headquarters, led the case, while the European Commission coordinated it.

title: Parliament passes medicine reforms, but drug prices stay with capitals
content:
Shortages and long waits for new medicines are what Europe’s biggest pharma reform in 20 years is meant to fix. Parliament approved it on Wednesday, together with the Critical Medicines Act. But the new laws leave drug prices with national capitals, just as pressure from US pricing grows.

In a plenary session on Thursday, MEPs urged the European Commission to stop member states from making their own deals with Washington. “Divided, we take the price. United, we set the terms,” said Stine Bosse (Renew/DNK).

They also asked what the Commission will do now. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, answered for the Commission. She did not say. Pricing stays with the member states, she said. She asked Parliament to pass the Biotech Act “as soon as possible”.

The debate came one day after Parliament gave final approval to the pharma package and the Critical Medicines Act (CMA). It followed a question to the Commission from Ms Bosse, on behalf of Parliament’s Committee on Public Health (SANT).

title: ‘Good intentions do not protect borders.’ New push for security boost in next EU budget
content:
More money for asylum and integration, tighter border controls and more effective returns, stronger internal security and greater solidarity among member states. These are the priorities shaping the European Parliament’s proposals for the EU’s next seven-year budget.

Three reports, three different priorities. And a bigger bill for the EU’s next multiannual financial framework (MFF). The European Parliament’s Civil Liberties Committe (LIBE) backed funding proposals covering migration, asylum and security policies.

But the proposals highlight the differing political priorities at play: while some lawmakers focus on tightening controls and returns, others insist that European migration policy must not be reduced merely to the defense of borders.

Lawmakers want to increase the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund to €13.31 billion. The European Commission had initially proposed €11.97 billion. The proposal also set aside two 15-per-cent shares of each member state’s allocation. One would go to the Common European Asylum System, including its external dimension. The other would support legal migration, integration, and social inclusion.

title: Battle of Kyiv: Decoding tomorrow’s summit Ukraine showdown
content:
One of the Union’s defining dramas is to unfold tomorrow and Friday. Europe’s Ukraine loan faces a stern Brussels test. What are the odds?

The story has all the hallmarks of a historic clash of titans, minnows, and everybody in between. European Council President António Costa has put Ukraine’s financing on the agenda for the special summit on Thursday and Friday. Leaders will also discuss the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, the EU’s long-term budget.

In Wednesday’s plenary debate, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen introduced the Ukraine package. She said: “We call it the Instrument for Coordinated Support for Ukraine. (Thus) Europe is covering two thirds of Ukraine’s financing need.”

The centrepiece is a Commission proposal for up to €45bn in additional support for Ukraine in 2027. Reports describe roughly €20bn for budget support and €25bn for military needs. The package would cover about two thirds of Ukraine’s estimated €70bn financing gap.

Who bears the borrowing costs is unsettled. Reporting says future interest payments remain unresolved and may affect the Ukraine allocation in the next budget.
snippet: One of the Union’s defining dramas is to unfold tomorrow and Friday. Europe’s Ukraine loan faces a stern Brussels test. What are the odds?
creator: Daniel Deyl
